cases.source_title: A new era for work
cases.content: A controlled trial found that a small language model handled routine support drafts well, but human review remained necessary for exceptions. The team recommends using AI for first drafts rather than autonomous decisions.

cases.source_title: How to reduce LLM inference cost?
cases.content: Serving benchmarks answer the cost question directly: 4-bit quantization halved GPU memory per replica, and continuous batching raised throughput 2.3x. Combined, cost per thousand tokens fell 61%, with a measurable quality drop only on long-context tasks. The authors recommend quantizing latency-insensitive batch workloads first.

cases.source_title: Does prompt caching hurt answer quality?
cases.content: The team asked whether enabling prompt caching degrades answer quality. Two short runs gave conflicting results: one showed no measurable difference, another showed a drop on multi-step questions. The sample was too small and the experiment was paused; no conclusion was reached.

cases.source_title: Shipping faster: our CI/CD story
cases.content: The team set a goal of cutting release time from two weeks to three days. They replaced the manual QA gate with an automated smoke suite plus a staged rollout. Median release time fell to three days and escaped defects stayed flat over twelve releases.

cases.source_title: I changed my mind about agent skills
cases.content: The speaker used to recommend preloading every available skill. After comparing agents with a global skill bundle against agents given one tool only when a concrete failure appeared, the larger bundle reduced task accuracy. The speaker now recommends adding skills only in response to a demonstrated need.

cases.source_title: Lifecycle-aware collection in Android
cases.content: The Android sample compares a collector tied to the Activity lifecycle with an unbounded collector. The lifecycle-aware version stops work while the screen is inactive and avoids a duplicate request when the user returns.

cases.source_title: A compiler feature changes Kotlin APIs
cases.content: The article demonstrates how Kotlin context parameters remove repeated plumbing from a library API. Its examples use a command-line program and do not involve Android, Jetpack Compose, or the Android SDK.

cases.source_title: Negotiate the offer, not the title
cases.content: The recruiter recommends comparing total compensation and asking for the written range before accepting an offer. The advice applies across professions and does not discuss Android engineering.

cases.source_title: Four inversions for smoother accompaniment
cases.content: The teacher shows how practicing chord inversions in the left hand reduces jumps between common progressions. The suggested exercise is to play each inversion slowly before adding the melody.

cases.source_title: Budget around irregular income
cases.content: The guide recommends building a monthly budget from the lowest typical income month, then directing any surplus to a cash reserve before increasing discretionary spending.

cases.content: The buyer's checklist adds maintenance, insurance, taxes, and closing fees to the advertised mortgage payment. It recommends comparing the full monthly housing cost before choosing an apartment.

cases.source_title: The tiny workflow trick teams missed
cases.content: In a short screen recording, the creator compares meeting notes made from an unstructured prompt with notes made from a fixed template. The template produced shorter notes with clearer owners, so the creator recommends using it for recurring meetings.

cases.source_title: A two-part agent workflow experiment
cases.content:
00:00 The speaker opens with a setup that many teams copy: one agent configuration with every available tool, skill, and instruction preloaded before any task begins. The argument for it sounds practical — the agent recognizes many commands, needs no discovery step, and never stops to ask which capability it should load. The speaker says this was their own recommendation for months, and the first half of the video explains why the approach felt productive.

08:00 Early demonstrations make the large setup look convenient. The agent answers a scheduling question, edits a document, and runs a small script without any routing logic. Each demo is short, the instructions are familiar, and nothing visibly fails. The speaker notes that these demos share one property: the task matches a capability that was already loaded, so the agent never has to choose between many plausible tools. Viewers see a capable assistant rather than the cost of carrying every instruction.

19:00 In repeated tasks on a fixed benchmark, the picture changes. Unrelated instructions consume the context window, and the agent misses explicit requirements more often because a plausible but irrelevant tool looks available. The speaker shows two runs with the same request: the preloaded agent picks a stale command and skips a required validation step, while the agent that loads one capability on demand follows the requirement. Accuracy falls as the bundle grows, even though every individual tool is useful in some other task.

24:00 The benchmark itself is modest: forty repeated tasks, two agent configurations, and a fixed checker that records whether each explicit requirement survived. The speaker shows one failure in detail: an unrelated deployment instruction is treated as relevant, the agent runs an extra step, and the required schema check is skipped. Across the run, the preloaded configuration completed fewer tasks correctly, while the on-demand configuration spent slightly longer selecting its one capability. The speaker argues the trade is worth it because a wrong action costs more than a selection step.

29:00 The final recommendation is to add a skill only after a concrete failure demonstrates the need, and to keep the default bundle small. The speaker repeats that globally preloading every skill performed worse in the experiment, and that the result is about task accuracy rather than latency. A short closing caveat says the benchmark covered tool-heavy coding and research tasks, so teams with mostly single-purpose flows may see a smaller difference.

cases.source_title: Why the pilot did not scale
cases.content: The article reports that a pilot cut response time but failed to reduce total support workload because exceptions still required manual review. The authors recommend limiting automation to routine requests until exception handling improves.

cases.source_title: Remote work pilot findings
cases.content: The internal policy document says the six-week pilot improved employee retention but did not change delivery time. It keeps remote work optional and recommends reviewing retention again after the next quarter.

cases.source_title: How reviewers read a diff
cases.content: The essay argues that code review catches design errors mainly when reviewers see a diff in small coherent slices. As the diff grows, review attention shifts toward formatting and naming, so architectural feedback disappears. The author's explanation is limited attention rather than reviewer skill.

cases.source_title: State in Compose: an overview
cases.content: A tutorial walks through three ways to hold UI state in Compose: view model state, rememberSaveable, and derived state. It shows tradeoffs but runs no comparison and gives no single recommendation; it suggests choosing by whether the state must survive process death.

cases.content: The article measures cold start after moving JSON parsing off the main thread with Dispatchers.IO. Cold start improved by 180 ms. The author notes that coroutines themselves were not the cause and warns the result does not apply to warm starts.

cases.source_title: Does a smaller context window hurt agents?
cases.content:
00:00 The speaker asks whether smaller context windows hurt agent reliability.

06:00 In a 200-task run, trimming irrelevant tool descriptions raised task success from 71% to 84%.

12:00 The conclusion: curating tool descriptions beat enlarging the context window, and the effect reversed when tasks required many tools.
